lesson.title: What a Function Really Is
lesson.summary: Introduces the function as a rule pairing each input with exactly one output, and shows why that "exactly one" requirement is the whole point.
lesson.body:
Imagine a machine with a slot for a number on one side and a tray for a number on the other. You drop a number in, the machine does something to it according to a fixed rule, and exactly one number comes out. That machine is a function. The number you feed in is called the input, the collection of all numbers you're allowed to feed in is called the domain, and the number that comes out is the output. What makes this machine trustworthy is a single strict promise: every time you put in the same input, you get the same output, and each input produces only one output, never two.

That promise is easiest to see with a concrete rule. Take f(x) = x², which means "take whatever number you're given and multiply it by itself." Feed in 3, and out comes 9. Feed in -3, and out also comes 9 ,  that's fine, two different inputs are allowed to share an output. But notice what can never happen: feeding in 3 can never sometimes give you 9 and other times give you 10. If a rule ever produced more than one possible output for the same input, it would fail to be a function, no matter how sensible or useful it seemed otherwise. This single-output requirement is why calculus can even ask meaningful questions like "how does the output change as the input changes" ,  if an input had multiple possible outputs, "the" rate of change at that input wouldn't even make sense to ask about, because there'd be no single value to track.

You can picture a function as an assignment between two sets: for f(x) = x², the domain could be all real numbers, and for each one, the rule points to exactly one number in the outputs. If you sketch this on a graph, with inputs along the horizontal axis and outputs along the vertical axis, the "exactly one output" rule turns into a visual test: any vertical line you draw should cross the graph at most once. For f(x) = x², a vertical line at x = 3 crosses the curve at the single point (3, 9), never at two different heights. Contrast that with a circle, like x² + y² = 1: a vertical line through x = 0.5 crosses the circle at two points, one above the axis and one below, so a circle is not the graph of a function of x. This is not a pedantic technicality ,  it's the same "one output per input" promise, just made visible geometrically.

It's also worth noticing that not every rule needs to be a tidy formula. A function can be a table of values, a description in words, or a graph, as long as the same one-output guarantee holds. For example, "assign to each day of the year the high temperature recorded that day at a particular location" is a perfectly good function, even though no algebraic formula produces it ,  each day genuinely has one recorded high temperature, so the assignment is valid. What matters for calling something a function is never how the rule is expressed, only that it never leaves an input's output ambiguous.

Keep this picture of an input-output machine in mind, because essentially everything ahead in calculus is really a question about functions: how their outputs change as inputs change, how fast they change, and how those changes accumulate. Before any of that can be asked, you need the function itself to be well defined ,  one clean output for every input you put in.
